questions.q: An n×n matrix A is diagonalizable if and only if:
choices: A has n linearly independent eigenvectors
every eigenvalue of A is nonzero
questions.explain: Diagonalization Theorem: A = PDP⁻¹ exactly when the columns of P are n linearly independent eigenvectors of A. Having n distinct eigenvalues is sufficient but not necessary (Examples 2 and 4 have a repeated eigenvalue and are still diagonalizable). Invertibility is a separate property.

questions.q: If A = PDP⁻¹ with P invertible and D diagonal, then every column of P is an eigenvector of A, and the i-th diagonal entry of D is the eigenvalue for column i.
questions.explain: Multiply both sides on the right by P to get AP = PD. Column i of AP is A v_i and column i of PD is λ_i v_i, so A v_i = λ_i v_i. Columns of an invertible matrix are nonzero, so each one is an eigenvector.

questions.q: Let P = [v_1 ... v_n] and D = diag(λ_1, ..., λ_n). Rewrite A = PDP⁻¹ as AP = PD and compare column i of both sides. What equation do you get?
questions.explain: AP = [A v_1 ... A v_n] and PD = [λ_1 v_1 ... λ_n v_n]. Matching column i gives the eigenvector equation A v_i = λ_i v_i.

questions.q: Which statements are true?
choices: A 5×5 matrix with 5 distinct eigenvalues is diagonalizable.
A 3×3 matrix with only 2 distinct eigenvalues is never diagonalizable.
Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are linearly independent.
questions.explain: Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues are independent, so n distinct eigenvalues give n independent eigenvectors. The matrix with rows (-7, -16, 4), (6, 13, -2), (12, 16, 1) has eigenvalues 5, 5, -3 and is diagonalizable. diag(0, 1) is diagonalizable but not invertible. The lower triangular matrix with rows (5,0,0,0), (8,-4,0,0), (0,7,1,0), (1,-5,2,1) has det -20, so it is invertible, but it is not diagonalizable.

questions.q: The matrix P in a diagonalization A = PDP⁻¹ is unique.
questions.explain: You can reorder the columns of P (and reorder D to match). You can scale any column by a nonzero number. For a repeated eigenvalue you can use any basis of its eigenspace. Check a different-looking answer with AP = PD before deciding it is wrong.

questions.q: The 2×2 matrix with rows (0, 0) and (0, 1) is:
questions.explain: The matrix is already diagonal (take P = I), so it is diagonalizable. Its determinant is 0 (0 is an eigenvalue), so it is not invertible. Invertibility depends on whether 0 is an eigenvalue. Diagonalizability depends on whether there are enough independent eigenvectors.

questions.q: If a square matrix has a repeated eigenvalue, it cannot be diagonalizable.
questions.explain: A repeated eigenvalue is fine as long as its eigenspace dimension equals its multiplicity. The matrix with rows (-7, -16, 4), (6, 13, -2), (12, 16, 1) has the double eigenvalue 5 with a 2-dimensional eigenspace, so it is diagonalizable. Only a shortage of independent eigenvectors makes a matrix non-diagonalizable.

questions.q: A has rows (97, 2) and (3, 98). Use λ² - (tr A)λ + det A = 0 to find the smaller eigenvalue of A.
questions.explain: tr A = 195 and det A = 97·98 - 2·3 = 9500. Then λ² - 195λ + 9500 = (λ - 100)(λ - 95), so the eigenvalues are 100 and 95.

questions.q: A has rows (5, -3, 0, 9), (0, 3, 1, -2), (0, 0, 2, 0), (0, 0, 0, 2). List its eigenvalues with multiplicity.
questions.explain: A is upper triangular, so its eigenvalues are its diagonal entries: 5, 3, 2, 2. The eigenvalue 2 has algebraic multiplicity 2.

questions.q: A has rows (-7, -16, 4), (6, 13, -2), (12, 16, 1). λ = 5 is an eigenvalue of algebraic multiplicity 2. Use the trace to find the third eigenvalue.
questions.explain: The eigenvalues, counted with multiplicity, add up to tr A = -7 + 13 + 1 = 7. So 5 + 5 + λ = 7 and λ = -3. Check with the determinant: 5·5·(-3) = -75 = det A.

questions.q: Which of these numbers are roots of λ³ - 7λ² - 5λ + 75?
questions.explain: Any integer root must divide the constant term 75, so test its divisors. 125 - 175 - 25 + 75 = 0 and -27 - 63 + 15 + 75 = 0. The polynomial factors as (λ - 5)²(λ + 3).

questions.q: A has rows (-1, 0, 1), (-3, 4, 0), (0, 0, 2). Column 2 of A is (0, 4, 0). What can you conclude immediately?
choices: e₂ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue 4
4 is the only eigenvalue of A
e₂ is in the null space of A
questions.explain: A e₂ is column 2 of A, which equals 4e₂. So e₂ = (0, 1, 0) is an eigenvector for λ = 4. The full set of eigenvalues is -1, 2, 4, which are distinct, so A is diagonalizable.

questions.q: The eigenvalues of the matrix with rows (-7, -16, 4), (6, 13, -2), (12, 16, 1) are its diagonal entries -7, 13 and 1.
questions.explain: You can read eigenvalues off the diagonal only for triangular matrices. This matrix is not triangular. Its eigenvalues are 5, 5, -3. They have the same sum as the diagonal entries (the trace, 7), but their product is det A = -75, while -7·13·1 = -91.

questions.q: A has rows (5, 0, 0, 0), (8, -4, 0, 0), (0, 7, 1, 0), (1, -5, 2, 1). The eigenvalue λ = 1 has algebraic multiplicity 2. What is the dimension of its eigenspace?
questions.explain: A - I has rows (4,0,0,0), (8,-5,0,0), (0,7,0,0), (1,-5,2,0). Working from the top gives x1 = 0, then x2 = 0, then x3 = 0, and x4 is free. That is one free variable, so the eigenspace is span{(0,0,0,1)} and its dimension is 1 (rank(A - I) = 3).

questions.q: Why is the matrix with rows (5, 0, 0, 0), (8, -4, 0, 0), (0, 7, 1, 0), (1, -5, 2, 1) not diagonalizable?
choices: λ = 1 has multiplicity 2 but only a 1-dimensional eigenspace
it has a repeated eigenvalue, so it cannot have 4 eigenvectors
it is lower triangular, and triangular matrices never diagonalize
its determinant is -20, so one of its eigenvalues must be 0
questions.explain: The eigenspace dimensions add up to at most 1 + 1 + 1 = 3 < 4, so A does not have 4 linearly independent eigenvectors. The repeated eigenvalue alone is not the reason: the upper triangular matrix with rows (5,-3,0,9), (0,3,1,-2), (0,0,2,0), (0,0,0,2) also has a double eigenvalue and is diagonalizable. det A = -20 ≠ 0 means 0 is not an eigenvalue.

questions.q: A has rows (-7, -16, 4), (6, 13, -2), (12, 16, 1), and λ = 5 has algebraic multiplicity 2. How many free variables does A - 5I have?
questions.explain: A - 5I has rows (-12, -16, 4), (6, 8, -2), (12, 16, -4). Every row is a multiple of (3, 4, -1), so the rank is 1 and there are 3 - 1 = 2 free variables. The dimension 2 matches the multiplicity 2, so A is diagonalizable.

questions.q: A 4×4 matrix A has characteristic polynomial (λ - 1)²(λ - 2)(λ - 3). Which of these facts, on its own, guarantees that A is diagonalizable?
choices: λ = 2 and λ = 3 each have a 1-dimensional eigenspace
questions.explain: Only the repeated eigenvalue 1 can cause a failure. rank(A - I) = 2 gives 4 - 2 = 2 free variables, which matches multiplicity 2. That is the same as a 2-dimensional eigenspace. Rank 3 gives dimension 1 < 2, so A would not be diagonalizable. The simple eigenvalues 2 and 3 always have 1-dimensional eigenspaces, so that fact decides nothing.

questions.q: For which values of k is the matrix with rows (1, k) and (0, 1) diagonalizable?
questions.explain: λ = 1 has multiplicity 2. A - I has rows (0, k) and (0, 0), which has two free variables only when k = 0 (and then A = I is already diagonal). For k ≠ 0 there is one free variable, so the eigenspace is only 1-dimensional.

questions.q: An eigenvalue with algebraic multiplicity 1 always has an eigenspace of dimension exactly 1. So when testing diagonalizability, only the repeated eigenvalues need checking.
questions.explain: For every eigenvalue, 1 ≤ dim(eigenspace) ≤ algebraic multiplicity. With multiplicity 1, the dimension is forced to be 1, so such an eigenvalue can never cause a shortage.

questions.q: Both matrices are lower triangular with eigenvalues 3, 3, 5. (a) has rows (3, 0, 0), (0, 3, 0), (1, 2, 5). (b) has rows (3, 0, 0), (1, 3, 0), (1, 2, 5). Which are diagonalizable?
questions.explain: (a) A - 3I has rows (0,0,0), (0,0,0), (1,2,2). Its rank is 1, giving 2 free variables, which matches multiplicity 2. (b) A - 3I has rows (0,0,0), (1,0,0), (1,2,2). Its rank is 2, giving only 1 free variable, which is less than 2. The eigenvalues are the same but the answers differ, so you must row reduce A - λI.

questions.q: A has rows (-1, 0, 1), (-3, 4, 0), (0, 0, 2). Which vector is an eigenvector for λ = -1?
questions.explain: A + I has rows (0,0,1), (-3,5,0), (0,0,3). This gives x3 = 0 and -3x1 + 5x2 = 0. Taking x2 = 3 gives (5, 3, 0). Check: A(5,3,0) = (-5,-3,0). The vectors (0,1,0) and (2,3,6) are eigenvectors for 4 and 2.

questions.q: Eigenvectors v1, v2, v3 of A have eigenvalues 2, -1, 4 respectively. If P = [v1 v2 v3], which D makes A = PDP⁻¹?
questions.explain: The i-th diagonal entry of D must be the eigenvalue of the i-th column of P. Sorting the eigenvalues without reordering the columns of P breaks AP = PD.

questions.q: A has rows (97, 2) and (3, 98). Which vectors are eigenvectors of A for λ = 100?
questions.explain: A - 100I has rows (-3, 2) and (3, -2), so -3x1 + 2x2 = 0. The eigenvectors are the nonzero multiples of (2, 3), including (-4, -6) = -2(2, 3) and (1, 1.5) = 0.5(2, 3). (-1, 1) is the eigenvector for 95.

questions.q: A has rows (-7, -16, 4), (6, 13, -2), (12, 16, 1). Which vectors lie in the eigenspace for λ = 5?
questions.explain: A - 5I reduces to the single equation 3x1 + 4x2 - x3 = 0. (1,0,3), (0,1,4) and (-4,3,0) satisfy it, and any two of them form a basis of the 2-dimensional eigenspace. (-2,1,2) is the eigenvector for -3.

questions.q: A has rows (5, -3, 0, 9), (0, 3, 1, -2), (0, 0, 2, 0), (0, 0, 0, 2). Which vector is an eigenvector for λ = 3?
To check a proposed diagonalization with P invertible, it is enough to verify AP = PD. You do not need to compute P⁻¹.
questions.explain: When P is invertible, A = PDP⁻¹ is equivalent to AP = PD (multiply on the right by P or by P⁻¹). Checking A v = λv for each column is the same check, done column by column.

questions.q: If A - λI row reduces with no free variables, then λ is not an eigenvalue of A.
questions.explain: λ is an eigenvalue exactly when (A - λI)x = 0 has a nonzero solution, which requires at least one free variable. Getting no free variables means an earlier arithmetic mistake. Never put the zero vector in P.

questions.q: If A = PDP⁻¹, then Aⁿ equals:
questions.explain: A² = (PDP⁻¹)(PDP⁻¹) = PD(P⁻¹P)DP⁻¹ = PD²P⁻¹. Each inner P⁻¹P cancels, so Aⁿ = PDⁿP⁻¹, and Dⁿ just raises each diagonal entry to the n-th power.

questions.q: A has rows (4, -2) and (1, 1). A = PDP⁻¹ with P having rows (1, 2), (1, 1) and D = diag(2, 3). Use Aᵏ = PDᵏP⁻¹ to find the (1,1) entry of A³.
questions.explain: det P = -1, so P⁻¹ has rows (-1, 2) and (1, -1). The (1,1) entry of Aᵏ is -2ᵏ + 2·3ᵏ. For k = 3 that is -8 + 54 = 46. Check by direct multiplication: A³ has rows (46, -38) and (19, -11).

questions.q: 100A = PDP⁻¹, where D = diag(100, 95) and P has rows (2, -1), (3, 1). Which of these is a diagonalization of A itself?
questions.explain: Divide both sides by 100: A = P(D/100)P⁻¹ = P diag(1, 0.95) P⁻¹. Scaling a matrix scales its eigenvalues by the same factor and leaves the eigenvectors (the columns of P) unchanged.

questions.q: If v is an eigenvector of A with eigenvalue λ and c is a nonzero number, then v is an eigenvector of cA with eigenvalue cλ.
questions.explain: (cA)v = c(Av) = c(λv) = (cλ)v. This is why A = (1/100)·[rows (97, 2), (3, 98)] has eigenvalues 1 and 0.95 with the same eigenvectors (2, 3) and (-1, 1).

questions.q: Suppose x₀ = c₁v₁ + c₂v₂, where A v₁ = λ₁v₁ and A v₂ = λ₂v₂. If x_(k+1) = A x_k for every k, then x_k equals:
questions.explain: Each application of A multiplies the v_i term by λ_i, so after k steps it has been multiplied by λ_iᵏ. Terms with |λ| < 1 die out, terms with λ = 1 persist, and terms with |λ| > 1 grow.

questions.q: For any square matrix A, you can compute Aⁿ by raising each entry of A to the n-th power.
questions.explain: Entry-wise powers work only for diagonal matrices. For example, if A has rows (4, -2), (1, 1), then A² has rows (14, -10), (5, -1), not (16, 4), (1, 1).

questions.q: Each year 3% of employed people lose their job and 2% of unemployed people find one. With x_n = (e_n, u_n) (employed, unemployed) and x_(n+1) = A x_n, what is A?
questions.explain: e_(n+1) = 0.97 e_n + 0.02 u_n (97% keep their jobs, and 2% of the unemployed are hired). u_(n+1) = 0.03 e_n + 0.98 u_n. Column j shows where group j goes, so each column sums to 1.

questions.q: Employment model: x₀ = (16.5, 1.2) million (employed, unemployed) and A has rows (0.97, 0.02), (0.03, 0.98). How many million people are employed after 1 year? Give 3 decimals.
Write x₀ = (16.5, 1.2) as c₁(2, 3) + c₂(-1, 1), where (2, 3) and (-1, 1) are eigenvectors of the employment matrix for eigenvalues 1 and 0.95. Find c₁.
In the employment model, x_n = 3.54(1)ⁿ(2, 3) - 9.42(0.95)ⁿ(-1, 1). What happens as n → ∞?
choices: the (2, 3) term dies out, leaving the (-1, 1) term
both terms die out, so x_n tends to 0
questions.explain: 0.95ⁿ → 0 while 1ⁿ = 1. So x_n → 3.54(2, 3) = (7.08, 10.62) million, which is 40% employed and 60% unemployed. The eigenvalue-1 eigenvector gives the steady state.

questions.q: Employment model: x₀ = (16.5, 1.2) million, A has rows (0.97, 0.02), (0.03, 0.98), with eigenvalues 1 and 0.95 and eigenvectors (2, 3) and (-1, 1). In the long run, how many million people are unemployed?
questions.explain: u_n = 10.62 - 9.42(0.95)ⁿ → 10.62. Equivalently, the total 17.7 million splits 2:3 along the eigenvector (2, 3): (3/5)(17.7) = 10.62.

questions.q: In the employment model, the long-run 40%/60% split would change if the same 17.7 million people started out divided differently between employed and unemployed.
questions.explain: Aⁿ → (1/5)·[rows (2, 2), (3, 3)], and every column of this limit is (0.4, 0.6). The long-run split depends only on the total population, not on the starting split.

questions.q: In the employment model, e_n = 7.08 + 9.42(0.95)ⁿ and u_n = 10.62 - 9.42(0.95)ⁿ. After how many years n do the unemployed first outnumber the employed?

A population moves by x_(n+1) = A x_n, where A has rows (0.9, 0.2), (0.1, 0.8) and x₀ = (30, 0) thousand (city, suburbs). The eigenvalues are 1 and 0.7, with eigenvectors (2, 1) and (-1, 1). In the long run, how many thousand people live in the city?
